unit.title: Light and shadows
unit.blurb: How shadows form, changing shadows, and transparent, translucent and opaque materials.

O1.t: Know that a shadow forms when an object blocks light, and that we need light to make a shadow.

O2.t: Change the size of a shadow by moving the object or the light, and know shadows change during the day.

O3.t: Sort materials into transparent and opaque, and choose materials for a job.

O4.t: Know that translucent materials let some light through, and sort materials into three groups.

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Can we make a shadow bigger or smaller? Let's find out!
This is lesson 3.2: changing shadows.
Put a torch on a table, shining at a wall.
Hold a teddy between the torch and the wall.
Move the teddy close to the torch.
Wow! The shadow gets big!
Now move the teddy away from the torch.
Move it close to the wall.
The shadow gets smaller!
Near the torch: big shadow. Far from the torch: small shadow.
Pause and think.
How can you make a shadow bigger?
Your shadow outside changes too.
In the morning, the Sun is low. Your shadow is long.
At midday, the Sun is high. Your shadow is short.
In the evening, the Sun is low again. Your shadow is long!
A shadow has the same outline as the thing that makes it.
A star makes a star-shaped shadow.
A triangle makes a triangle-shaped shadow.
But a shadow has no colours. It is just dark.
Did you know?
Long ago, there were no clocks.
People looked at the shadow on a sundial to tell the time!
Riddle time!
You can run as fast as you like, but you can never jump on its head. What is it?
Your shadow!
Your turn.
When is your shadow shortest?
Let's draw shadows!
In the morning, stand a toy on a big paper outside, in the sun.
Draw round its shadow.
Come back after lunch, and draw round the shadow again. Has it changed?
Let's remember.
Move an object near the light, and the shadow gets bigger.
Move it far from the light, and the shadow gets smaller.
Outside, shadows are long in the morning and evening.
And short at midday. Super shadow work!

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Can light go through everything? Let's find out!
This is lesson 3.3: transparent and opaque materials.
Look through a window.
You can see the trees and the sky outside!
Light goes straight through the glass.
Glass is transparent. Transparent means see-through.
These materials are transparent.
Window glass and a drinking glass.
Clear water.
And cling film. You can see through all of them!
Pause and think.
Which material is transparent?
Some materials do not let any light through.
Wood, brick, metal and a thick book.
You cannot see through them at all.
We call them opaque. Opaque materials make dark shadows.
We choose materials for their jobs.
A window must be transparent, so we can see out.
A door is opaque, so nobody can see in.
Thick curtains are opaque. They keep the light out at bedtime!
Did you know?
Some jellyfish are transparent.
You can see right through their bodies!
Riddle time!
What can go through a window without breaking it?
Light!
Your turn.
Why are windows made of glass?
Let's do a torch test.
Collect some materials: cling film, a book, a glass and some foil.
Shine a torch at each one. Does the light go through?
Sort them into transparent and opaque.
Let's remember.
Transparent materials let light through. You can see through them.
Glass is transparent.
Opaque materials block all the light.
And opaque materials make dark shadows. Crystal-clear work!

stops.note: Paused on the “Pause and think” card.

stops.note: Paused on the “Pause and think” card.

captions: Hello, little scientists!
Some materials let a little light through. Let's meet them!
This is lesson 3.4: translucent materials.
Look at a bathroom window.
It is bumpy, or cloudy.
Light comes in, so the room is bright.
But you cannot see clearly through it. Everything looks blurry.
Materials like this are translucent.
Translucent materials let some light through.
But not all of it.
Hold tissue paper up to a window. Light comes through, but you cannot see clearly.
Pause and think.
What does translucent mean?
These are translucent.
Tissue paper, and a thin plastic bag.
Frosted glass.
And a paper lantern. It glows softly!
Now we know three groups.
Transparent materials let all the light through.
Translucent materials let some light through.
Opaque materials let no light through.
Did you know?
Shine a torch through your fingers in the dark.
They glow red! Your skin lets a little light through.
Joke time!
Why was the window so good at hide and seek?
Because nobody could see it!
Your turn.
Which material is translucent?
Let's sort materials!
Collect tissue paper, cling film and card.
Hold each one up to a window. Is it clear, blurry or dark?
Sort them: transparent, translucent or opaque.
Let's remember.
Translucent materials let some light through.
Things look blurry through them.
Tissue paper and frosted glass are translucent.
Transparent, translucent and opaque. Brilliant work, little scientists!
